subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, June 6, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to encourage the provision of intermediate term and short term credit to farmers for the improvement and development of farms through bank loans, guaranteed with limitations, by the crown; moneys payable under the act including expenses of administration to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
While I think the principle of the proposed bill for guaranteeing individual farmers up to a maximum of $3,000 may be a step in the right direction, yet at this stage I have one or two observations to make and some questions on which I desire some enlightenment. When the parliamentary assistant was completing his argument on March 14 on the Industrial Development bank bill he said:
I find it a little difficult to see why the credit requirements of agriculture should be so different from those of industry that they should require a government central farm bank to operate in cooperation with private lending institutions.
The parliamentary assistant thought these two desires were very much in common at that time. In the first place, I believe that legislation with respect to floor prices for agricultural products have a great deal to do with the success or otherwise of this proposed bill, and I think it is unfortunate that the proposed legislation has not been before the house earlier than this. Had it been, it would have been very useful, when this proposed bill is being considered by the banking and commerce committee, which I believe is the intention. These two will be very closely associated if this proposed bill is to mean anything to agriculture.
If farm credit is to be on a sound basis the interest rate should be considerably less than five per cent. Many farmers are to-day receiving credit from the banks at five per cent. True enough, credit was not procurable at this rate of interest in many sections of the country some years ago, but many good farmers to-day are procuring such credit at five per cent. I have not been able to learn
[Mr. Fair.l
yet why it is necessary to have a separate industrial bank, supplementary to the activities of the existing lending agencies, while this proposed bill is for a limited guarantee of farm credit through the existing chartered banks, as I have pointed out; and the parliamentary assistant expressed himself similarly in winding up his argument on the industrial bank on March 14.
I am not able to recollect whether any suggestion as to interest rate in connection with the industrial bank has been mentioned. If the minister could enlighten us in that regard it would be appreciated. I should like him to tell us what the proposed rate of interest will be in that connection because it has a bearing on this bill. I have pointed out before that the Veterans' Land Act does provide an interest rate of 3i per cent in connection with land for these settlers.
This proposal to guarantee the banks is really just an extension of the provisions of section 88 of the Bank Act. In my opinion that is all it amounts to. I know personally a number of old people with substantial farm homes in areas where the Canadian farm loan board would not lend money a few years ago. These old people found it necessary to apply for old age pensions. These pensions are now a lien against these farm homes and in some cases the farm is now operated by the younger members of the family. I would ask the minister whether these people now operating these farms will be allowed the credit guaranteed under this proposal for home improvements while the lien applies against the farm home. I would also ask him whether this guarantee of ten per cent will cover the total loans of each chartered bank or each branch which carries individual loans or the individual loans themselves.
I have heard arguments about the interpretation of the wording. It is pointed out in the minister's statement that:
It is .proposed that the guarantee should foe effective in respect of a maximum of $250 million of loans made within a period of three years. Apart from this over-all limitation on the
Government's liability, there will foe provision or termination of the guarantee after due notice on loans in any particular category or made by any particular bank. This will ensure effective control over lending operations.
I am not very clear on that. For instance, there will be quite a number of loans taken out and loans may be repaid in a very short time. I wonder whether those loans will be included in the total, or whether it is the total over the given period, or whether it might be pro rated eighty-three and a third million dollars a year. On that point may I say to the minister that when we entered the war there

Farm Credit
was a backlog of requirements of farm implements alone of 8200,000,000. I am sure it will be all of $250,000,000 now. In fairness I do think many farmers will not have to take advantage of this guarantee in order to purchase implements, but we have been slipping away back in requirements of farm implements every year during this war and there will be a tremendous amount of money required for that alone, apart from the fact that there is a very great need for an improvement in live stock in this country.
With respect to live stock, I was surprised to note that in this great dairying province of Ontario butterfat production among Holstein cattle alone had declined on the average from I think 3-3 to 2-6 per cent over the past period of some years. I was amazed when I learned that. It certainly proves that we have to do something about the improvement of live stock. Many people in the west have never had an opportunity to procure better type sires to improve their stock, as they should have done.
A question was asked the other evening as to the interpretation of what was a farm. The minister said:
It is intended that .a farmer shall mean a person who is in possession of a farm, and whose principal occupation consists of farming such farm. Then "a farm" is defined to mean land used for the purpose of farming, which term includes live stock raising, dairying, fruit growing and all tillage of the soil.
This brings to mind the fact that in past years many difficulties were encountered in the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as to just what was considered a farmer by the treasury board. Many payments were held up at times because of the difficulties connected with a proper interpretation of what was forthcoming from the treasury board. I trust this matter will be very carefully taken care of in the drafting of the bill, because it is most important and many unnecessary inconveniences have been created.
As I said, I think this bill is a step in the right direction. I am sorry that we did not have the bill before us, but there was some little misunderstanding the other evening between the minister who was leading the government and others as to where we could properly ask questions. I did not want to lose the opportunity to raise the questions which I have asked of the minister. I hoped in the earlier discussions in the house when the proposed legislation with respect to agricultural credit was mentioned, that it might have been on a broader basis which would permit many agriculturists to rewrite their obligations at a lower rate of interest. I realize that
we have other measures such as the Canadian farm loan board. I think they make provisions for loans on lands and chattels. The minister has pointed to the success of the national housing plan. Might I remind him that in most sections of rural Canada, in the west at any rate, that plan never applied, and there is a great need of something of that kind in the rural sections. Therefore the success of this measure can hardly be based on the success or otherwise of the national housing plan.
I trust I may have an opportunity to ask further questions when the bill is before us, but I should like to have an answer to the questions I have already asked, if I may.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
The resolution which is now
before the committee on which the bill is to be introduced later is a proposal for a measure that has for some time been looked for by Canadian farmers. If we understand the intention of the government with respect to this measure I think it is to fill a need in agriculture that has been looked forward to for a long time.
The principle of the bill, as I understand it, is that loans are to be made for improvements on farms, taking in practically all activities of the farm, but more particularly having in mind improvements with respect to buildings, machinery, fences, live stock, improved seed and even buildings such as homes and other permanent structures. I note that emphasis has been placed on electrical equipment. Electrical equipment is one thing farmers are looking forward to with particular interest at this time. If that is what is intended by this measure then it can be considered as filling a place that has been needed for some time. The rate of interest is five per qent. I understand that repayments are to be made on a basis that will be suitable to the particular type of agriculture for which the loan is being made. That is one of the important things that should be kept in mind-the obvious ways and means over a widespread type of agricultural activity either by regulations or otherwise that will permit the type of repayment suitable to the particular industry that is being undertaken.
I point out, however, in considering this measure which is to be administered through our regular chartered banks, that there is a little difficulty in this country in the service which this type of loan will give to certain communities. We have not been doing very much to increase the banking facilities, par-, ticularly in western Canada. In fact there has been a substantial reduction in the number of banks in the west. I find in the report of the reconstruction committee that this is substantially the case and that our banks have
Farm Credit

been reduced from 4,620 in 1920 to 3,300 in 1941. Our banking facilities are largely centred in the larger towns and cities. I wonder whether the minister has taken into consideration the outlying areas where banking facilities are nut provided by our chartered banks as they exist at the present time. That is one matter to which consideration should be given. The other point to which consideration must be given is with respect to the administration. I quite appreciate that ldans of this kind will depend a great deal upon the personal element, both from the point of view of the encouragement given by the bank manager to these loans and from the point of view of the individual who may borrow under this scheme. I do not know what the minister has in mind, but I hope he can draft some sort of regulation that will meet this problem, because it is going to be one of the most important that will have to be considered.
As the hon. member for Souris has already pointed out, the farmers are supplied with one type of credit through the Canadian farm loan board; that is long-term credit and, in some cases, short-term credit as well. I do not think we should get away from that system for the more substantial, permanent requirements of agriculture; that is, having longterm loans repayable on an amortization basis over a period of years at a rate of interest as favourable as that provided in this measure. The other type of credit that has been available in the past, of course, has been whatever loans farmers could make from their banks. I take it that the credit now proposed is to fill the gap between these two, and to take the place of the credit previously provided by merchants, lumber dealers, implement dealers and people of that kind. I point out that this is a new avenue of approach with respect to legislation of this type, and I believe it should commend itself favourably to agriculture.
Some people may ask whether this type of credit is needed at this time in the history of Canadian agriculture. In that connection I should like to make just two references. One was made by the minister in introducing this measure the other evening, namely, the report of the agriculture committee on reconstruction which, after making a general survey of the needs of agriculture, in the closing subparagraph recommended:
. That the dominion government make a careful survey of the schemes for providing short-term and intermediate credit now in force in other countries, with a view- to making provision for adequate credit at low rates of interest to deserving farmers, using as far as possible existing facilities, including the chartered banks of Canada.

I presume that recommendation was brought forward after very careful study, and after hearing representations made by a large number of people. If the policy can be made to operate successfully, using the banking institutions, as we hope it may, then we shall have the advantage of not being required to create any additional facilities for this purpose. I find also that in the spring of this year, in the representations made to the government, the Canadian federation of agriculture also referred to this matter, and I should like to read part of the introductory paragraph dealing with farm credit:
The first is the subject of farm credit. The international food conference at Hot Springs recognized the importance and necessity of adequate credit facilities in any soundly conceived programme of farm improvement. It recommended that every effort be made to ensure an adequate supply of credit for agriculture at low rates of interest.
I point out that the Canadian federation of agriculture, which takes in all the farm organizations of Canada, not only adopts this recommendation as its own but refers to the conference held at Hot Springs early this spring, which would indicate that the need for credit of this kind apparently is recognized even outside our own country. Then, after some reference to the work of the Canadian farm loan board, and the possibility of reconsidering the introduction of the central mortgage bank, the federation goes on to recommend:
That a plan be developed suited to the nature and requirements of agriculture in Canada for short-term and intermediate loans. In this connection it must be remembered that there 'has been a steady reduction in the number of branches of chartered banks in Canada. At present, for example, there are only 170 branches in the whole of the settled area of Alberta. After taking into consideration the numbers in the cities and larger towns, it is evident that such a number cannot adequately serve such a large area. The very nature of farm production in Canada makes short-term and intermediate credit a necessity in the post-v-ar years.
I merely mention this to indicate that the Canadian federation of agriculture have been urging the adoption of a policy which would provide a type of intermediate credit. In the pamphlet they have sent out, dealing with their activities as an organization, they make further reference to the need of some type of short-term or intermediate credit.
There is no doubt in my mind that during the period of transition from war to peace agriculture will afford a great deal of employment and a means of rehabilitation, so that anything we as a parliament can do to assist agriculture undoubtedly will help our rehabilitation programme. I doubt if

Farm Credit
there is a farmstead in Canada which does not need repairs of some kind. Buildings require paint; fences need repair; new buildings are necessary. Then when we look at the other side and see the encouragement that has been given to the use of electrical equipment on the farm, I think we begin to realize the importance of a measure of this kin,d. I would point out that in regard to the purchase of new equipment alone agriculture will be of great benefit as far as employment is concerned, which in turn will be of untold advantage in stabilizing agriculture itself.
A moment ago I mentioned that to a degree at least the credit facilities largely used in agriculture in western Canada have been provided by implement companies, lumber dealers and country merchants. The hon. member for Souris referred to the backlog of agricultural implement requirements in 1937, at which time it was estimated to amount to more than
8200,000,000, plus an annual requirement of about $50,000,000. That situation may have improved to some extent in the years following 1937, but I doubt if it can be very much better to-day because of the shortage of farm implements due to war conditions. Therefore I believe that we have at the present time in this country a very great need for new agricultural implements, which doubtless will be the reason for a great many loans of this kind.
Just here I should like to say one thing to the minister, to which I hope he will give particular attention. I go back to the inquiry in 1936 and 1937 into the cost of farm implements. One of the matters particularly looked into at that time was the cost of credit sales and collection costs by implement companies in connection with the sale of farm implements, and a great deal of criticism was expressed. I do not wish to repeat the figures which were quoted at that time; I do not think they would be applicable to-day, and for that reason might be misleading.
The committee ended its report by stating that the cost of credit to farmers purchasing farm implements on time is excessive, and that the companies-meaning the implement companies-should take immediate steps to reduce credit charges. My point is this, that if through this measure the government is to provide a type of intermediate credit, and assume a risk through a ten per cent guarantee to banks, then the implement and lumber companies, and those who have provided goods to farmers on credit and who now have the advantage of this type of credit, should be *called upon to reduce their distribution costs as far as possible. I say that because they will be able to do business on a cash basis without much risk.
So I say to the minister that in this regard I think he should go a long way, if there are no other means available, towards putting it up to implement and lumber companies, the two groups which will likely receive a very large share of the advantage from this type of credit, so to adjust their businesses that will reduce their cost to a lowest possible minimum for the advantage they will secure under this type of credit.
The same applies to suppliers of electrical equipment. In Manitoba at the present time we have under way a survey for the extension of the hydro electric system of that province to a greatly enlarged area. This measure should assist in the development; I hope it will. If it does, I believe a further step should be taken to see that the goods so provided will be provided on the basis of a cash sale, with the lowest possible cost to the farmers concerned.
I note with satisfaction, too, that this measure is to provide loans which will permit even the building of a house up to a value of $3,000. Here I believe is an opportunity to offer a suggestion which in my view would go a long way toward assisting in the stabilization of agriculture, particularly in western Canada. My suggestion is to encourage the building of a second home for hired help on many of our western farms. There is no doubt that hired men have been more or less transients in western Canada. They have summer employment, but they have never been given a permanency such as an industry like agriculture should provide for its workers. I believe that the hired man has not been treated as well as he should have been, and that as a result the industry has suffered because of its not being able to maintain in employment experienced labour. I therefore offer this suggestion in the belief that it would be a permanent development and should be given sympathetic consideration, so far as the regulations and other governing factors in connection with these loans are concerned.
The same should apply with respect to water development in farm homes. However, at the moment I shall not deal with that feature in detail.
Another point which I suggest should be kept in mind when dealing with this measure, and one which I believe would be of great assistance, is that connected with the cooperative movement. Cooperative movements in western Canada have been making sound and rapid progress. For the most part they have operated in a wholesale of bulk type of business, but they are rapidly entering the retail field. There is no doubt at all that these cooperative organizations have demonstrated that they have lowered many of the costs of
Farm Credit

distribution. Some of them are trying to get into the farm implement business, and I hope they succeed. In the type of business they have undertaken they have, in my judgment, reduced substantially the costs of distribution and, for that reason, should be encouraged. So that, in so far as this type of credit may be made available to people who are associated with cooperative organizations, I think it is commendable.
I am also wondering with respect to our credit union movement, which is also a wide and, I think, a sound development in many areas. It does not, of course, cover the western provinces to the extent of providing the general credit facilities that would be required. Nevertheless the credit unions have made fairly rapid progress. Their idea is partly one of thrift; but on the other hand they are also providing a type of community credit which is of particular advantage to the communities using it. I hope the type of credit indicated in this measure can be made to fit in with the type I have just mentioned, because I believe there is something in common between them, and something which should be encouraged.
I have no further suggestions to make to the minister at the moment, except to point out again that in my view this is a measure which will fit into a place for which there is a need. It will fit into a place between the long-term loan, such as is given on a farm mortgage, and the short-term seasonal borrowing. If we are to have this type of credit to meet the intermediate needs of agriculture, I think it is desirable. This is just another example of making national credit available to meet the needs of a certain branch of agriculture-national credit, in the first instance, through the Canadian farm loan board, and now national credit by way of a guarantee of this type of intermediate loan.
I think, when one considers what has been made available to agriculture, it will be realized that considerable progress has been made in meeting its credit requirements. When one reviews the situation, particularly as it obtains at this time, one cannot help realizing that the credit facilities now offered are much more readily available to meet the needs of the industry than they were heretofore. I point, for instance, to the Canadian farm loan board. I look, as w'ell, at the wide development of the credit union movement. I look at the wide distribution of victory bonds, a further evidence of the available credit and now this new type of intermediate credit. So that, if, along with these credit facilities we can develop added security, through the
IMr. Weir.]
establishment of floor prices, the credit needs of agriculture should be pretty well taken care of.
At the same time a word of caution might be voiced. I am not one who thinks we should take steps to give an endorsation or an invitation to go out on a borrowing expedition, merely for the sake of borrowing. To my mind debt is a serious thing, and so far as possible should be avoided. So that while this measure is desirable and needed, it should not be taken as an invitation for farmers to go into debt. That is not the intention of the measure. I desire to commend this legislation, because in my view it will fill a place of great importance in the post-wrar period in helping to establish agriculture on a sounder basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I will deal with the questions that have been asked in so far as I can remember them. That is a lot of money, but if the plan was working well and the money ran out I assume that future parliaments would take such steps as they thought were in the public interest to increase the amount available.

The two hon. members from Manitoba who preceded me have asked some questions I had intended to ask, and the minister has already answered them. I should, however, like to know whether the minister intends to include a crop failure clause in the bill which will shortly be introduced. Such a clause is absolutely essential. Because of the troubles which the western farmer has experienced, not only in the distant past but right up to the present time, he has had to pay some small loans three and four times over. The situation which the minister mentioned with reference to cream separators is pretty well taken care of to-day by the
Farm Credit

farmer himself, by the establishment of credit unions; but so far as other loans are concerned, which are perhaps a little larger and extend over some time, I am sure the minister understands the difficulty a farmer finds himself in when, having agreed to pay for something in three years, he gets two bad crops in succession, and has nothing with which to pay, no matter how anxious he is to meet his debts. There should be added to the proposed bill or incorporated in it a crop failure clause whereby things would stand until a crop comes along.
Regarding interest rates, I am disappointed that the figure of five per cent has been mentioned. Mr. Donald G. McKenzie, of Winnipeg, speaking before the reconstruction committee, asked for adequate credit at low rates of interest to deserving farmers. To-day I or any other farmer in Manitoba can go to a bank and get credit at five or six per cent.

This part of the measure will be of no advantage unless the interest rate is lowered. I do not know what amount of research the minister has done into conditions in other countries which have established cheap agricultural credits; but, as Mr. McKenzie pointed out, it is essential that we have cheaper credits, or service at cost, the government providing for what profit is necessary. The minister said that "earnings must be sufficient to cover the bank's costs of operation and to give them an incentive to go out after business." The banks are to have their profit first.
The minister also said that this is a thorny problem and that the government intends to initiate discussions with the leading companies at once so that suitable agreements can be worked out in advance of the coming into force of the act. The minister there refers to the agricultural implement companies and the banks. I am sure that these organizations not only see the writing on the wall, but see it in neon lights-that the farmer, by organizing and building up more and more strongly his credit unions, is going to be a menace to the banking system in the operation of short-term credits. The implement companies at the same time see the threat of Cooperative Implements Limited coming along after the war. No doubt the banks and the implement companies are anxious that legislation of this kind shall go through.
I ask the minister, where do tenant farmers come in on this list? Most of them are men who lost their farms in the thirties and are anxious to be reestablished in the various provinces. I understood the minister to say

some time ago that a measure would be introduced to cover the case of farmers and fishermen. Will the farmer who fishes in the winter come under this measure, or will he have to wait until the legislation with respect to fishermen becomes law?
Regarding live stock, I hope that when the arrangements are put into motion they will apply not only to pure bred live stock but also to grade animals; because it would be all right for sires to be pure bred, but so far as dairy cows are concerned it would halve to apply to grade animals.

There is no crop failure provision in the bill as drafted. That matter can be considered by the banking and commerce committee. I do not know whether such a provision would be practicable or not. speechtext:
While I support the principle of this measure for the provision of intermediate term and short-term credit to the farmers of this country, I believe it would have been better if the minister had not written it into the Bank Act. In my opinion the proposed bill will be serviceable in a great many cases, but it looks to me as though the guarantee principle of ten per cent will make the chartered banks of this country a farm development finance corporation. Every good citizen has always supported very liberal terms for the farming community, protection all along the line; measures such as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and

Farm Credit
many other forms of assistance, through bonuses, subventions and subsidies, have commended themselves to the country. The provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act were afterwards applied to fishermen. I [DOT]contend that the measure now before us should also have included provisions for industrial *workers. The experience of the minister has borne out what I felt from the start would be true as regards the home improvement loans, of which the banks advanced 855,000,000 from November, 1936 to October, 1940. The government guaranteed up to fifteen per cent, but in fact every dollar was paid. It was a very wise proviso, and I hope it will now be extended because it is of particular value in urban and suburban areas, whereby also financial aid by the banks was promised for the stocking of fuel by consumers, the consumers placing orders with the coal dealers and the bankers advancing the money repayable each month. That has been a magnificent success; there has been only one bad debt. The minister gave a very fine statement on Tuesday night as regards these new forms of loans.
As hon. members know, I_have contended for many years that there has not been very liberal treatment to the man who has a small retail store which is subject to war-time controls, or to the small manufacturer or small wholesaler. I have very little hope after the discussion in this chamber that the proposed industrial bank will ever meet the situation so far as the retailer, the manufacturer and the wholesaler who are in a small way of business are concerned.
I am sorry that the minister has not seen fit to announce a liberal extension of the Home Improvement Act. Thousands of houses are needed not only in the urban and suburban areas but in the country as well, and we are not going to catch up with the shortage unless we do something definite about it. When this measure goes to the banking and commerce committee I should like to see this matter considered so that arrangements can be made for small house building on a long term policy for advancing money through the banks or by means of some amendments to the Home Improvement Act, whereby an equivalent amount of $250,000,000 could be provided for a period of from three to five years, for the purpose I have indicated, as the government is providing under the amendments to the legislation before us.
At page 3608 the minister said:
For these reasons it is proposed that the guarantee should be effective in respect of a maximum of $250,000,000 of loans made within a period of three years.
I should like to see that extended to take in small houses for soldiers, and white-collar
workers and industrial workers, a large number of whom are soldiers, so that they might be enabled to acquire small houses under the Home Improvement Act, at a reasonable rate of interest of 5 per cent. The minister said further at page 3609:
It is interesting to observe that the subcommittee on agricultural policy of the advisory committee on reconstruction, headed by Donald G. McKenzie of Winnipeg, in its final report recommended:
"That the dominion government make a careful survey of the schemes for .providing short-term and intermediate credit now in force in other countries, with a view to making provision for adequate credit at low rates of interest to deserving farmers, using as far as possible existing facilities, including the chartered banks of Canada."
I quote again from the minister's remarks, at page 3608:
First, as to purpose: the object of the scheme is to provide the credit needed by farmers to increase the efficiency of their farming operations and to enable them to make their farm homes more comfortable and attractive. With this in view, it is proposed that the guarantee should apply to loans made for the purchase of farm implements and farm equipment, for rural electrification, for the purchase of live stock, for fencing and drainage, for the repair, alteration and construction of farm buildings and for other farm improvement purposes that may later be specified in the regulations. The categories are very broad and include nearly every kind of permanent improvement to a farm or farm home.
Then he goes on to speak of eligibility for loans. I submit that instead of writing paragraphs f, g, h and i, of subsection 1, into the new Bank act, the same arrangement could have been made, as in the case of the home improvement act, and the same purpose achieved by making an agreement accordingly with the chartered banks, which are now before parliament seeking a ten-year renewal of their charters.	[DOT]
I am glad to see that something is being done with regard to the electrification, of the farms. One of the greatest achievements of the Ontario hydro electric scheme, under Sir James Whitney and1 Sir Adam Beck, was that it brought the joy of living to the farmers of that province through the electrification of the rural areas. In Sir Adam Beck's own bams, on almost the first power secured, I saw the use of electricity fully illustrated. As I say, the electrification of the farms in Ontario brought to the farmers the full joy of living that electricity gave to the people in the cities. Now that that has been accomplished on a large scale in Ontario with rural lines by direct subsidy, the rural sections of the province have been given at very low cost electrical service for all the requirements of the farm.
I am sorry to see the proposals with regard to the Bank Act so far as real estate is con-
Farm Credit

cerned. I refer particularly to sections 82 and 88, the latter being amended by this particular resolution. By section 82 it is provided that no bank shall hold real estate or movable property except such as is required for its own use. The building must be commensurate with the size of the business, and no bank is allowed to erect a building of thirty or forty stories. This provision, however, is circumvented by having some lawyer draft an agreement for some kind of holding company, indirectly and, as I said, illegally. In that way the section is got around. By section 82, with regard to real estate, any bank property such as I have described is held for seven years and after that it reverts to the crown and anyone can bring action to have that section enforced. But there are large buildings and skyscrapers all over Canada.
As regards section" 88, I think it is very dangerous to open up the Bank Act to the extent proposed. We have the Macmillan report for guidance, and I can find in that report nothing that would justify the very wide open door we have here. Many of the provisions of the proposed legislation will alter the whole basis on which these loans are made. In Toronto there are seventeen trust companies, many loan companies and corporations, insurance companies, the chartered banks and the shark loan companies. Under this legislation I should like to see every industrial worker, small retailer, small wholesaler and small manufacturer given some relief from the system of shark loans. I should like to see the shark loan companies wound up and liquidated and the work they are carrying on transferred to the chartered banks or the industrial bank or come under a new measure like this one, or under the Home Improvement Act, so that there might be equality of treatment as between farmers and urban and suburban workers and the small manufacturer and retailer, in regard to credit. If that were done there would be no more two per cent per month, or twenty-four per cent per annum, for all these small people to pay. The shark loan companies are exploiting the small man, and I submit that we should also do everything in our power to protect from these agencies the soldiers who are coming back. I suggest that an agreement could have been made with the banks.
I hope the banking committee will consider what I have said here and elsewhere many times and put the people to whom I have referred on a basis of equality with other classes in the community, who are now preferred. There is one thing about the present Minister of Finance, and I will say this in his favour. I am glad to see that he has not

overlooked committees of the house, as the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) does. That minister seems to be a law unto himself when it comes to some of the bills in which he is interested. The Minister of Finance, on the other hand, is quite willing to meet a committee of the house and he does not mind having the proposals of his technical officers examined by any committee. Not so the other department to which I have referred. The rules of the house should be amended accordingly to apply to all such large proposals.
I will say this in conclusion, that there is great demand that something be done by the banks and by the government in connection with housing, including the farms. Under the definition of land everything is included up to the skj'-buildings, farms, everything else. No doubt the same definition will be given under the amendments to the act. I venture to say that when some of those loans are applied for, (he chartered banks will insist, under section 88 and others, on collateral security. They will insist that agreements for sale, mortgages and othci forms of collateral, such as deeds [DOT] and insurance policies, be deposited with them, so that in the event of the loan not being paid those deposits can be liquidated. I believe that will prove to be so, and it will be so in so far as the Industrial Development bank is concerned.
When the committee considers this measure I hope that it will consider whether we should open this door wide open for real estate investments by banks and make what should have been arranged by agreement, part of the Bank Act. Once this gets into the Bank Act you will never get it out; it is there to stay. In any revision ten years hence paragraphs (f), (g), (h) and subsection 1 and so on included in this measure will remain.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
I am in general agreement with the purposes of this legislation and I wish to commend the minister for introducing it. I think all parties are in agreement with the purpose. Most agriculturalists from my part of Canada have not so much difficulty in getting credit, although in many instances it is needed. What they require more than credit is a satisfactory market for their production. Our farmers should" have earnings at least fifty per cent greater than they have been able to obtain over a period of years in order that they might be prosperous enough to avail themselves of the new credit facilities that will be provided by this measure.
I notice that it provides for the financing of agricultural implements. Costs of agricultural implements in Nova Scotia are too high.

Farm Credit
I believe they are greater than in other parts of Canada. I know they are greater than in central Canada. Central Canada gets the benefit of producing those agricultural implements, the benefits of wages, material, and all the incidental business that goes with them, while we pay the higher cost. On Monday a return was brought down at my request with respect to the higher cost of bicycles in the maritime provinces. What applies to bicycles applies to agricultural implements as well. I would say that, in fairness to the maritime provinces, prices of bicycles and prices of farm machinery should be uniform. The people of Nova Scotia should not have to pay a higher price than the people of central Canada.
The return to which I referred shows that a man's bicycle costs in all parts of Ontario and Quebec 842.50. Some parts of those provinces have just as expensive a freight rate as the maritime provinces. A lady's bicycle costs $43.50. What do we find in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island? A man's bicycle costs $45, and a lady's $46, or $2.50 per bicycle additional, about five and a half per cent more.
It is my view that farmers and others in the outlying parts of Canada who do not have the benefit of the labour, material and business that go with the production of farm implements, bicycles and articles of that kind they require, should at least be accorded the same price when they have to buy them and they should not have to pay higher prices.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: You will never get that from Ontario.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
This measure will also provide for additional financial facilities for the improvement and construction of new buildings. That is fine. We are all in favour of that; but I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that he should at the same time take the sales tax off the cost of lumber, paint and other supplies that go into the cost of these farm buildings. Interest on the loans will amount to five per cent; the sales tax is eight per cent. That means a cost of thirteen per cent added on to the materials that go into these farm buildings; therefore the farmer is not able economically to borrow the money and make such investments, because the cost is too great, unless the sales tax can be removed. If the farmer wishes to build a henhouse or an addition to his barn or his house or to supply storm windows the cost is eight per cent for sales tax, and if he has to borrow the money he must pay five per cent, which makes a charge the first year of thirteen per cent. I would say, Mr. Chairman, that an undertaking on
the part of the minister that the sales tax will be removed on farm improvements should go hand in hand with this measure. If that cannot be done during war time an assurance should be given that the sales tax will be removed immediately on the termination of the war when we expect these new financing provisions will be made use of to assist the farmer and give employment to help reestablish many returned men after the war. This legislation will be a benefit not only to farmers all over Canada but to workingmen and merchants in the towns and cities and to manufacturers generally. I make that suggestion to the minister. I am in favour of this legislation. And I think it will be appreciated by the agriculturists, but I think it should go farther than the terms of the proposed bill.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
I think all hon. members of the committee will support the general principle of this legislation. It is advisable to provide for allowing farmers easier credit conditions for medium and short-term loans, but I think we must not overlook this important fact, that the fundamental difficulty we are going to face in the years during the war and in the post-war period is that of purchasing power in the hands of the people to enable them to buy the goods which the farmers are able to produce. Thus far the minister has not brought in any measure designed to provide such purchasing power. That is an exceedingly important matter. If there is not sufficient purchasing power in the hands of the people of Canada to enable them to buy the goods which the farmer produces, then there will be the grievous danger of a fall in prices; and if the prices of the product that the farmer produces, and the markets fall low enough, then these loans will be unrepayable. All that they will do is constitute a millstone round the necks of the farmers. All through the western Canadian provinces we are suffering grievously because the farmers obtained credit when there were reasonable prices for products and then were required to repay the loans when the bottom had fallen out of the market. Thus far there is simply no provision before parliament to prevent the bottom from falling out of the market. Of course it is suggested that the government propose floor prices. We have no idea how high those floor prices are to be. What precaution is to bq taken against the floor prices being so low that the farmers, after they have paid the cost of production, will be unable to make a living on the farm?
My general criticism of all the minister's measures thus far is along the line I have indicated; there is not sufficient provision for internal purchasing power to enable the people
Dominion Elections

to buy the goods which the producers of Canada will be able to produce in abundance, and there is no adequate provision for fixing prices which will be remunerative to the producers.
May I now turn to a matter which came up just before the dinner recess The minister asked what could be done to make sure that the farmers in any given area would be able to obtain loans, following the remarks of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay who asked how the government were going to provide that farmers in every area would be able to obtain loans. I should like to offer this suggestion, that one good way to help attain that objective will be to permit the creation of provincial banks. No governing body in the Dominion of Canada is more concerned about seeing that the farmers in Nova Scotia obtain loans than is the government of Nova Scotia, and the same is true with respect to every province in this dominion. If you want to be sure that the farmers in any particular area are going to have the opportunity to get the credit they need, one way to bring about that result will be to allow the provinces to have provincial banks. Let the minister bear that in mind when he comes to consider the petition of Alberta for a provincial bank. I believe one great difficulty that has been developing during the last three or four generations in Canada is the centralization of the control of credit. That control must be decentralized. The credit union has done a good bit toward helping farmers in local areas to get credit, but the credit union is too small to accomplish the total objective, and its development is rather too slow. I have all respect for those who advocate credit unions; I know something about them and appreciate their value, but this whole matter of the control of credit must be put into the hands of the people whose interests are directly concerned. I submit that to have the control of the credit of Saskatchewan placed in the hands of a group of men living in Ontario and Quebec is not likely to provide the credit needed in Saskatchewan.
Perhaps anything else I have to say can be said at a later stage of the bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I should like to say a few words. This resolution presages a piece of legislation as important as almost any piece of legislation we shall have passed this session, outside the war appropriation bill itself. If the minister is in position to give some statement while the legislation is in the resolution stage, the house would appreciate it as well as the country. We should have a statement with respect to the government's policy and what the bill proposes to do. The question of the distribution and sale of surplus crown assets is one which is engaging the attention of the whole nation at the moment because of the present situation. Could the minister oblige the house by giving a full statement at this stage?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the procedure for the disposal of surplus crown assets has been worked out over a short period. It was set up by order in council and we have had some three months in which to assay the efficiency of the programme. First, there is the determination of surplus property. This determination is made by a surplus crown assets committee which is made up of representatives of each of the departments of government which is concerned with the disposal. The membership of the committee consists of representatives of the three armed services, of the Department of Public Works, of the Department of Pensions and National Health, of the Department of Munitions and Supply, of the Department of Trade and Commerce, of the Department of Finance and of one or two others. In addition there are representatives of the farmers, of labour and of the consumer. The committee is a policy committee.
Surplus Crown Assets

Anything that any department may declare to be surplus is reported to the committee. The representatives of the government on the committee are senior civil servants of the rank of deputy minister or assistant deputy minister. The material is reported as surplus to the committee and the committee decides, first, whether the material should be disposed of and whether it is really surplus to government requirements. The various departments of government are represented and if a department can show that it can usefully use the material, this is noted by the committee.
The committee represents various walks of life and various departments of government and it recommends the policy that shall be followed in the disposal of the article. The matter is then referred by the committee to the Minister of Munitions and Supply with the recommendation, first, that the property should be disposed of and, second, as to what priorities should be given. These may include the provinces, the municipalities, and the various public agencies or otherwise as a means of disposal to the public. The recommendations of the committee are noted and an order in council is prepared.
The recommendation is made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply to council that the property should be disposed of, and as to the various priorities that should be recognized in the disposal of the property. If council approves the disposal of the particular property the title passes to a corporation known as War Assets Corporation. This is a corporation in the ordinary form. Its directorate includes business men of varied experience and a representative of labour, whose composite judgment cover the field of disposal in many avenues. The president is a man who has been with the Department of Munitions and Supply' as director general of its Washington office since the commencement of the war; before that he was an experienced contractor and president of a steel company, a man with wide experience in purchasing various materials and one who has a good knowledge of the avenues of disposal.
The material or equipment passes to this corporation. The corporation is bound by the recommendation which goes forward to it from the committee at Ottawa, as to priorities. It may be material or equipment which should be rendered into scrap; if so, it is rendered into scrap through the agency of the corporation and sold as scrap. If it is possible to recondition the material or equipment and sell it in its original state, that is carried out.
The corporation will have a number of advisory committees. These will be formed as required, and the advice of the industry' within
' 
which the material falls is asked. It may not alway's be followed, but at least it is at hand as a guide. If the material can be used in its original form, the purpose of the corporation is to make that material available as widely across Canada as possible. Motor cars, for instance, are not offered for auction in one city; a price is placed upon them and they are shipped to various centres in Canada and sold, so that each section of the country may have the same opportunity as any other to buy. If it is scrap it is sold on the scrap market at a ceiling price imposed by the wartime prices and trade board. That board, by the way, is represented on the disposal committee, and its advice is sent forward together with the advice of representatives of the department and representatives of the public that I have named.
The experience to date is on a limited scale. Hon. members will realize that, while disposal in future will be a job of the greatest magnitude, at the present time it is fairly limited, but experience is being built up through such use as is being made of the machinery at the present time. When the bill is before the house for second reading I will table a report of the disposal on machinery up to the end of May which will give hon. members a fair idea of the methods used to date and the results obtained. Our experience so far is such that I believe that the machinery provided by the bill which is now being brought before the house will be the best that can be devised for the huge job of disposal which will follow the end of hostilities. When the bill is before the house we shall be able to discuss the machinery in detail. I may say that the study of disposal in this country runs parallel with the studies being conducted in the United States. Our machinery was set up some months before the machinery was established in the United States, but it is a matter of interest to me that the disposal in that country operates almost exactly in the manner which had previously been established for Canada. Those responsible for the disposal in Canada work closely with those similarly responsible in the United States. The methods are compared, and if it is a matter of export the opinion of the United States is obtained, just as the United States obtain the opinion of Canada if they have material to export.
We have exported a considerable amount of surplus material under very satisfactory arrangements. Later on, the scope of the' disposal must be extended to the United Kingdom. Obviously a great deal of Canadian material will have to be disposed of in that country, and we are conducting studies with the United Kingdom government

Surplus Crown Assets
to make sure that the methods for disposal of Canadian materials shall parallel the methods which will be established in Great Britain.
I do not know that I can usefully say anything further. I shall be glad to answer any questions, but I suggest to hon. members that we can most profitably discuss this subject when the bill is before the house.

speechtext:
According to a dispatch in one of the evening papers, a debate took place in the old country parliament to-day, when an hon. member called the attention of the Prime Minister to what happened after the last war in the matter of purchase of German ships, an operation which, according to the hon. member, resulted in great disasters to employment in the British shipbuilding industry. The hon. member asked the Prime Minister if such a condition would prevail after the present war. The Prime Minister intimated that many mistakes were made after the last war, but this was one which would not be repeated.
In looking over the resolution, I notice that the corporation which is to be set up is to be authorized to "sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of, hold, manage, re-condition, or otherwise deal with surplus crown assets." I have been wondering whether such a committee should not have some authority over the buying of scrap material or other material from other countries, because we shall have a large amount of material to be sold in this country, and we have plants here with a capacity far beyond our peace-time requirements, plants which will have to be demobilized in an orderly way. This I know from what I personally have seen in the plants I visited, and it seems to me that the proposed bill should call for some control over buying, too, whereby dealers in Canada would not be permitted to purchase huge stocks of cheap material, whether in Great Britain, the United States or elsewhere, and throw them on our home market. After the war, our own plants will return to their normal peace-time production; their own workmen will have to be protected, and I cannot see any other way to do so than by some control over buying. The minister said nothing about that, or I would not have risen. But I remember clearly what happened after the last war, when the business with which I was associated bought many steel boilers which were used in this and that plant, and then-

speechtext: You had better be careful.	,

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am always careful. I do not say anything I do not know. The
firm bought many steel boilers and afterwards sold them at prices below those for which boilers of a similar capacity could be purchased from the home manufacturers. That must have had an effect on boiler production and naturally on the employment in our boiler plants. So that as far as I can see, unless there is some control over buying as well as over selling munition materials, the situation as a whole will not be taken, care of. As the minister has said, in. the United States they are planning and setting up a body which will to the best of their judgment carefully watch that the market is not glutted in any way and that employment is not retarded through the placing on the market of equipment which will have such effect.
The minister said something about cars. It would be an exaggeration to say that there are hundreds of thousands of motor cars stacked up across the country, but undoubtedly there is a large number. The minister did mention motor cars distributed across Canada, and we shall all be anxious to get the motor car companies engaging in that line of manufacture and everything associated with it, and the thousand and one concerns making equipment for motor cars must be got back into peace-time production as quickly as possible. If the market throughout Canada is to be glutted with thousands of war motor cars, which naturally would be sold cheaper than would cars made in the regular plants, that, too, will affect employment, will it not?
I for one will support the proposal. I have heard the names of the men who will head the company. I am not at all in favour of government companies, but I believe that this is one that possibly could manage to do a good job. In any event it will be expensive, and it will call for control to see that the market is not glutted with war material. Having heard the names of the men who are to look after the affairs of the company, I have confidence in them. They are men of great experience. The chairman, whom the minister mentioned, has had vast experience. I doubt if you could select a more capable man in the country. The others also are good men, and I have no doubt they will do the best job they can.
I do not remember clearly what programme operated after the last war. I do not think it was very good, but perhaps it was not very bad. I will not say anything against it apart from what I have said about buying used equipment for resale. But may I ask the minister this question: Has he in mind any control over the buying of material from the United States or Great Britain or from any other producing country, Australia or elsewhere, so that our market shall not be flooded
Surplus Crown Assets

with competition of surplus war goods? The minister spoke of sending our surplus goods to Great Britain. According to a debate in the British House of Commons to-day, they will take care that their market shall not be glutted with goods from other countries, and I presume that our cousins to the south of us will do the same. I am anxious that Canadian plants will not have their production retarded through competition with huge used stocks from other countries, because I want the Canadian workmen to be given the best possible opportunity to produce when the war is over. I ask this question: Has the minister in his mind some control over buying outside war surpluses?

The experience the government will have in connection with these crown plants will follow the experience we had after the great war and other wars the world over in connection with a venture like this. I do not hesitate to say, Mr. Speaker, that the country will never get any reasonable return on the investment involved and some crown plants should have been left to private enterprise. The minister hopes to make a deal with regard to the surplus assets and he confers on the corporation power to spend more capital and to dispose of, hold, manage and re-condition these plants. Again I say they will never have any reasonable return on investments in the past or from the proposed policy of the government in the future in regard to captial advanced. Many of these undertakings have been constructed in an uneconomic way and they have dragged in some municipalities in the building of certain roads, sewers, pavements, water supply and all that sort of thing. I have seen some of the crown plants and I do not believe that business of this kind can be run on an economic basis. When the war is over, a great many of them will be obsolete and not worth much from a commercial point of view. They will be uneconomic, and it will not be possible to operate some of them commercially. Many of them will be worthless. We had an experience of that in the last war with the merchant marine. We constructed many plants throughout Canada and some ships cost SI,750,000. They ran all the way from SI ,000,000 to S2,000.000 What was the result? About a year before Munich the present minister of the department sold without tenders some of them for $50,000, although

they cost $1,750,000. There was a return with a list of them made to an order of the house along that line. I doubt very much whether we shall ever get any reasonable return on some of these investments. If more capital is put into it after the war I venture to say that less will be got out of the total investment in the future than in the past.

speechtext:
I am pleased that the minister is forming this Crown Assets Corporation to take charge of this material after the war, because I can see where a company of this kind can be of good service to the country. I do not agree with some of the suggestions that have been made here to-night to the effect that this material should be turned over to private concerns to sell at prices which they may set. It is government property and the government should take the proper steps, as the minister has indicated, to dispose of it.
I want to join in what the hon. member for Souris said a few moments ago about the disposal of some of this machinery. I received a resolution passed by the board of trade of the city of Drumheller with regard to this very thing. I am sorry I have not the resolution here to put on Hansard or read to the minister; but its contents are to the effect that these municipalities are desirous of obtaining some of this machinery, especially road machinery, from the assets corporation. They figure, and I think rightly so, that they will be able to get this machinery at very reasonable prices. They are of the opinion that some of this machinery will be of use to them in the construction of roads and for other purposes, and they are quite concerned about it. It may well be that some of this machinery will be practically new, or it may be, as the minister has indicated, that some of it can be repaired with very little trouble and be made very useful to the municipalities and other organizations of that kind.
I think it is proper that arrangements should be made with other countries, as the minister has indicated, so that there will be no dumping of great quantities of machinery into Canada from the United States or from Canada into other places. Let each county dispose of its own surplus material in its own way. I just wanted to mention this and to give what support I could to it along with what other hon. members have said, because municipalities are very much concerned about getting possession of some of this machinery which will be useful to them. I think the minister should indicate in a circular letter, or something like that, to the municipalities or cities that such action is being taken and, if they wish to get in touch with him, he will acquaint them with the
methods of obtaining the desired material. I think that would be of great assistance to them and would give relief to what means a great deal to them.

I am very glad to see that the minister is setting up this corporation. If we did not have some corporation of this kind we would have chaos in this country. It depends to a great extent on how it is managed. The minister has said that up to the present time the machinery has been successful. I think it has been only moderately successful. There is a great deal of improvement necessary. I have great faith and confidence in the manager who, I understand, is Mr. J. B. Carswell. I have known him for many years. He is a man of great patriotic spirit, a man who could have looked after himself much better in this war if he had not been patriotic. He is a man of great ability. He is a Scotsman, by the way.
I want to see this government corporation get back to private enterprise as quickly as possible. There is only one way to judge efficiency and that is by competition. At the present time we know that some of our government plants have done splendid jobs, but we do not know at what expense. We are bound to have extravagance in war time; there is no question about that. But in peace time you cannot have efficiency and extravagance; it just does not work out. The only way you can gauge the efficiency of a firm is by the competition it meets. There are so many controls of one thing and another to-day that private enterprise no longer obtains. There is only one thing that is worth while in the production of ordinary goods and that is private enterprise. That is the way to do it. I do not say that everything should be private enterprise. We must have a combination of private and public enterprise. After all, the government is here to help private enterprise, not to run private enterprise. The sooner we get these industries back into the hands of private enterprise after the war, and not run them as government concerns, the better it will be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am pleased with the acclaim with which this legislation has been received on all sides of the house, but I think lurking in the back of everybody's mind is the desirability of this, and primarily that is because of the hon. gentleman whom we all know or hope and believe will be the responsible minister of the crown administering this measure, and the company which is being set up. I refer to none other than the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). It is the fact that he has
Surplus Crown Assets

done such a remarkable job in his present capacity and is likely to have charge and supervision of this measure which gives us so much confidence in what this company will be able to do in the disposal of our surplus assets. In my own home city we have already had concrete proof of what a government department can do in converting a war-time asset into civilian use and employment. Nothing could give us more confidence in Calgary as to the future success of this corporation than the demonstrated ability of the present minister who is responsible for this legislation.
But there is the thought to which the hon. member for Davenport gave expression, which was uppermost in my mind, namely, the possibility of the disposal in this country of surplus assets of other countries to the detriment, if you like, of our own corporations or to private industry in Canada. We are all well aware of it. I personally have had brought to my attention already the difficulties which may be encountered in that respect in Alberta, I believe that certain surplus assets of a friendly neighbouring country are being offered for sale. I have already had it brought to my attention that certain associations in the United States are encouraging or bringing pressure to bear to have surplus assets of that country disposed of as secondhand material in Canada, to use Canada as a dumping ground to get rid of those assets so as to clear the field for their activities in their own country. I am very much concerned as to what effect that is to have, and while I well understand the anxiety of municipalities, provincial governments and local authorities to get equipment and machinery especially, after all, private enterprise, the people who have been handling and dealing in machinery and equipment and who will be expected to maintain it and to provide repairs for it in the years that are to come, would like to know what position they are to be left in.
We in this county are now educated to look to the manufacturer of any implement or machine to guarantee performance. The trade mark, trade name or manufacturer's name, when impressed upon a machine, does mean something; and the person who buys that machine looks to the manufacturer to maintain it in good working order. Take a piece of road building machinery, for example, that has been used on the Alaska highway under most trying conditions, operated by inexperienced or perhaps incompetent workmen, without proper maintenance, because speed was the prime consideration. That piece of equipment may look all right, but it may be full of defects not apparent to the ordinary

purchaser. Is that to be put on the market as a bargain and sold to the highest bidder for whatever it will bring in its present condition, under the principle of caveat emptor, or let the buyer beware? That piece of equipment may look to be worth $5,000, while in reality it may need repairs or replacements costing $2,000. Who is to service it; who is to be responsible for it?	I can see the
possibility of great harm and damage to Canadian industry unless this matter is very closely supervised. The minister said that at the present time there is a gentleman's agreement with other countries. I hope there will be something a little more definite than that; otherwise I fear we may have this country flooded with the surplus used material of a friendly neighbour, who will be glad to get rid of it at prices which we in this country cannot afford to meet.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mrs. Casselman in the chair.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CORPORATION AND ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like the minister to make it clear whether crown assets include buildings and crown companies as well as such movable things as automobiles, jeeps and so on, which have been mentioned already. Then that recommendation comes back to the government, and nothing can be disposed of except by the decision of the cabinet. Therefore, whether the Polymer corporation or any other corporation will be disposed of depends entirely upon the government of the day, and as long as we maintain good government in Canada I hardly think the Polymer corporation will be disposed of.

Referring to the discussion that took place before the house went into committee, I should not like hon. members to believe that the sole duty of this disposal corporation will be to prevent surplus material from interfering with the manufacturers of this country. That

Surplus Crown Assets
will be one duty; but it must be remembered that the surplus material from this war is the property of the people of Canada, and must be disposed of in the interests of the people of Canada, having due regard to the situation of the manufacturer and the effect on employment. The practice is to price the material reasonably, having in mind the value of similar material newly manufactured. None of this will be sold as a pig in a poke; it will be sold either as scrap or as usable material. It will be properly priced and distributed as well as possible, so that if it is useful to the people of Canada it will be obtainable in all sections of the country at a price representing fair value in comparison with the article when new.
I may say that an effort is being made to give priority to various users. For material such as road-building equipment, which has been mentioned, and which I may add has not come on the market as yet for the reason that the limited quantities in Canada are still needed for war production work, the first option would go to the provinces, then to the municipalities and then to any other public use for which there might be a requirement. However, the price is the same for all. That has been determined as a policy, and I think it is the only sound policy. We have resolutions coming in suggesting that certain users should obtain property as a gift, or at a lower price. All we can give any user is a first claim on the material; but once the price is fixed that will be the price to all. I am glad to have this opportunity of making that fact known to all those who have written me, and others .who say we should offer one price to one and another price to another.

ties of shell-making machinery were just smashed up and made into scrapiron. They were single purpose machines and they could not be used for anything else.
