subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866

speechtext: Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services) moved the second reading of bill No. 112, respecting the naval service of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: Does the minister propose to make a statement at this stage?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
I
should be glad to make a short statement on the principle of the bill. This is a measure to amend and consolidate the Naval Service Act, which was first passed in 1910 and which now appears as chapter 139 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. In all the years since the first Canadian naval legislation was passed there have been but three very minor amendments of the act; and that, I think, is a'tribute to the vision of those who laid the foundation for the service we know to-day. However, needs and conditions have changed, and under
the acceleration provided by war conditions some changes are necessary and some of those changes ought to be made, I think, immediately.
The existing act was passed before Canadians had any extensive knowledge of naval warfare and before Canada had any fleet of her own. We can now lay claim to some considerable practical knowledge of naval affairs and naval administration. We find that some procedures required by the present act are rather clumsy; certain other procedures are inconvenient; still others are obsolete entirely.
The passage of the amendments which are proposed to the house will enable the naval authorities to reduce the great mass of legislation in one form or another which is now applicable to the naval service of Canada. At the present time the service is governed by a complex body of Canadian and British acts, regulations and orders which can be integrated only with the utmost difficulty even by legal specialists. I may say that there is no comparable complexity in the Royal Navy or in the United States navy, the two services with which we are best acquainted, and that is so mainly because the legislation applicable to these two great services is designed to fit their own requirements. With these amendments we hope to accomplish a similar result for the Canadian naval service.
The house probably will be surprised to know that the provisions applicable to the Canadian service are to be found in no fewer than eleven different sources. Eight of these are Canadian and three from the United Kingdom. Thus to understand properly the conditions governing the naval service one would have to know first of all the Naval Service Act. In the second place, one would have to be familiar with the Canadian naval regulations, then with Canadian naval orders, three volumes, then with the Canadian confidential naval orders, then with the regulations affecting the fleet reserve, then with the regulations affecting the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, the regulations affecting the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, and1 finally the regulations affecting the W.R.C.N.S., or the Wrens as the organization is usually called.
There is a total of eight different sources to which one would have to look for the Canadian authority governing the naval service. But that is not all. Through the operation of section 45 of the present Naval Service Act, the following laws and regulations of the United Kingdom are in operation in so far as they are applicable to the Canadian service, and these United Kingdom regulations and laws are superimposed on all the
Naval Service Act

Canadian laws and regulations which I have mentioned. These United Kingdom laws and regulations are: The Naval Discipline Act of Great Britain passed in the year 1866, a fairly extensive act in itself; then there are King's Regulations and Admiralty Instructions, which are to be found in three volumes, and which contain something like 2,000 odd sections; and finally there are the Admiralty Fleet Orders, which up to the present are comprised in eight volumes.
That is a tremendous bulk of material for the personnel of the Canadian naval service to become familiar with, and in addition to that there is always the problem of deciding the application of this British legislation to situations that arise in the Canadian navy. There exists, as a further and very practical and pressing problem, the question of the constitutional right of Canada to adopt any part of the laws and regulations of the United Kingdom merely by future reference, as section 45 of the Naval Service Act of Canada proposes to do. Section 45 of the Naval Service Act states that the Naval Discipline Act of 1866, and the acts and amendments thereof passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom "for the time being in force," and so on, shall apply to the naval service. Now that phrase "for the time being in force" has given rise to considerable constitutional discussion in this country, and opinions have been given that no amendments or regulations passed since our statutes were revised in 1927 can be applicable at this time.
That is a brief outline of some of the difficulties. How do we propose to cure them? It is hoped that once the Naval Service Act of Canada is amended we shall be able to embody the Canadian law and the Canadian regulations in two volumes. First of all there will be the King's Regulations and Instructions for the government of the Canadian naval service, and that will be known by the short title of K.R. Can. (Navy). Then there will be, secondly, the Naval General Orders.
The amendments I am proposing by this bill will accomplish two general purposes. First, the amendments will affect some of the sections of the present Naval Service Act. These amendments will leave as much as possible of the present act untouched, and the changes suggested will merely be to simplify the administration of the act in the light of practical experience.
The second purpose that we have in mind is to provide Canadian legislation comparable with the British Naval Discipline Act of 1866. That purpose is carried out in part if of the bill, and the sections in this regard are to be found beginning on page 11 and

going on to the end of the bill. They are largely, almost entirely, simply an adaptation of the provisions of the British Naval Discipline Act, with a few minor changes to make the British provisions conform to Canadian terminology and Canadian legal practice.
I am of course in the hands of the house with regard to this bill, and I shall be glad to have any suggestions that may come from any quarter as to the proposals advanced.

The purpose of the first part of this amending bill is thus to revise that act. The Royal Canadian Navy has passed through so many exigencies in that time, it has grown so magifi-cently, particularly in these latter years, that I can well understand the difficulties which have been entailed in endeavouring to administer the navy under the succession of pieces of legislation such as the minister has announced.
The introduction of the second part, in which the Naval Discipline Act of 1866 is replaced by part II of this bill, appears to me to be an admirable way of dealing with the situation. There is no reason at all, since the passing of the Act of Westminster, why we should turn any longer to the legislation of the United Kingdom, useful and helpful though that has been to us in the past. It is the minister's proposal that we shall dispense with all of that and incorporate in one bill, the Naval Service Act, all the necessary legislation. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
The treasury board considers the matter and passes its minute which is approved by the council as a whole. The treasury board has not the final word in these matters.
On section 7-Chief of the Naval Staff.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: Is the chief officer in the British service and in the United States service a rear admiral?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: No; they are of higher rank. It says, "not lower in rank, than rear admiral." His title is now changed to "chief of the naval staff" instead of "director of naval services." That has been the title ever since I came here and I think it is a much better one.

Item agreed to.
On section 8-Permanent naval force.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: Is the minister in a position to give us any more details than he did during the discussion of his war appropriations, with regard to plans for a permanent navy after the war?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
I
think I intimated at that time that there was authority from the cabinet to have a navy of some eight or nine thousand men after the war. That is the only authority we have, and I cannot add anything to what I said when the war appropriation bill was under discussion.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: I suppose it will depend upon how far Canada commits herself in connection with the world organization with respect to an international police force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
I
fancy that would have some bearing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: That was the understanding arrived at some years ago, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: The complement was arrived at in 1941.

Section agreed to.
Progress reported.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, June 9, 1944
